claims.quoted_text: Since there are only 21 distinct powers of 2 but 4068289 squares, it is impossible to assign a different power of 2 to each square.
claims.explanation: This is false because there are infinitely many powers of 2; the problem imposes no upper bound on the final entries. Having finitely many squares does not prevent assigning distinct powers of 2. A correct obstruction would use parity/color-sum constraints on the bipartite grid.

claims.quoted_text: In such a tournament, any set of 2017 players can be dominated by the player ranked immediately higher than the highest-ranked player in the set.
claims.explanation: In a transitive tournament, if the chosen set contains the top-ranked player, there is no higher-ranked player to beat that player. Thus the proposed construction does not have the required property, even though tournaments with this domination property do exist via probabilistic constructions.

claims.quoted_text: However, the exact form of the bound \(\max(|A + A|, |A \cdot A|) \geq c|A| \log^2 |A|\) is not generally known to hold for all sets \(A\).
claims.explanation: This is false. The sum-product theorem gives a much stronger bound: there exist constants C,δ>0 such that max(|A+A|,|A·A|) ≥ C|A|^{1+δ} for all finite A⊂Z. This implies the stated |A| log^2 |A| bound, after adjusting c for small sets.

claims.quoted_text: For \(k = 7\), \(2^7 - 1 = 127\), which is much smaller than 1093. Therefore, it is not possible to partition \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 1093\}\) into 7 sum-free subsets.
claims.explanation: The condition n ≤ 2^k - 1 is only a sufficient construction, not a necessary bound. In fact 1093 = (3^7 - 1)/2, and [1,1093] can be partitioned into 7 sum-free subsets by a standard Schur-number lower-bound construction.
